rationale: This is essentially the archive's "Demand-Funding Capex Gap" with the coverage denominator changed from lct to capx, a cosmetic rescaling that also introduces a badly behaved ratio (oancf/capx explodes and flips sign as capx approaches zero or is negative), so any change in results will be hard to attribute to the stated mechanism.

Firm-demeaning both legs of the strong level-based inventory/cash-coverage imbalance is a substantive change in information content (abnormal vs. persistent liquidity quality) rather than a rescaling, though there is a real risk that the earlier alpha came precisely from the persistent level/distress component that this construction removes.

Adding a prior-leverage gate is an economically motivated conditioning that plausibly separates consequential recapitalizations from routine liability reduction, and the sign is internally consistent, but the triple MIN conjunction will thin the tails and coverage, so a weak-but-noisy alpha is a plausible outcome.

The construction is close to a sign-flipped variant of the archived "Unexplained Capex Instability" (swapping ib-volatility for sale-volatility) and, because the dominant driver of the score is high sales-productivity volatility, the expected negative sign largely restates the known earnings/sales-volatility anomaly rather than testing the claimed investment-rigidity channel.

This is a rescaling of the already-tested Equity Proceeds Absorption Gap; the self-normalizer is bounded but blows up toward ±1 for firms with negligible issuance and uses, so it risks trading transaction-magnitude sensitivity for small-denominator noise without a new economic mechanism.

Only the normalization of the maintenance-gap leg changes relative to the archived "Liquidity-Supported Maintenance Alignment," making this an incremental robustness variant whose bounded ratio becomes unstable when both capex and the accumulated-depreciation change are near zero.
